extracted.intended_audience: administrative analysts and managers in government agencies (public administration practitioners and students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing, estimating, scheduling, and controlling administrative work loads and sequences in large organizations (with examples from REA, Forest Service, TVA). Focuses on methods for time standards, backlog, reporting, and production control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate time by average or standard time (convert to man-hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating is done by determining an average or standard time for accomplishing each unit and converting to man-hours. This process is an essential part of estimating and is done by contractors and manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for setting production costs or bidding construction jobs; administration usually charged to overhead or allocated pro rata. In large administrative organizations with supervisory, executive, and research activity, measurement of time is necessary to find true costs and time requirements and has led to executive workload measurement and scheduling techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop work units for standardized manual and clerical tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Work units for standardized manual and clerical tasks can usually be developed without great difficulty and may be evaluated by direct time study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When item size and difficulty vary but general character remains, obtain average time values by inspecting work records, file copies, counting production, or direct time studies; assign standard time to runs when variation is measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use work records or diaries when direct time study impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct time study is not feasible, average times may be obtained by inspecting work records or keeping count of production; accurate work records (diaries) reduce uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some organizations (notably the Forest Service) urge keeping diaries. Inability to apply a stopwatch is not a deterrent provided sufficient leeway is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow estimation by experience and occasional judgment for novel jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: When work varies in character or a brand-new job appears, it is necessary to estimate on the basis of experience and occasionally to resort to outright guessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make tentative estimates and correct as circumstances warrant; periodic stock-taking by executives reduces risk of overpromising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain an all-round picture before setting time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Before trying to set a time estimate for any job, it is necessary to get an all-round picture of it using analysis by function, by unit of organization, and by sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the factors/questions suggested in earlier chapters (Loveridge's questions) to ensure adequacy of data for estimating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Loveridge's questions in workload analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the set of questions (Purpose/Necessity; What and Who; Method/Assignment; Where/When; Contribution of tasks to administrative end; Possibility of combining similar tasks; Coordination; Work load; Personnel; Conditions of motion; Accomplishment; Balance of qualitative factors) as an analytic checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These headings provide a concrete checklist for specific use in work load analysis to ensure the analyst knows what jobs are about even if he cannot perform them all personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce individual and group workload estimates including motion delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Work load analysis produces load estimates for individuals (necessary for proper work distribution) and approximate times required for performing each task; these may be compounded into group work load estimates and times for entire projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include suitable allowances for motion delay when compounding times into group or project estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create standard time lists and identify control points
rubrics_metrics.description: After job times are determined, make a standard list showing them in order and showing the time after allotment when each should be completed; designate key actions as 'control points'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a standard timetable for sequences (example: REA time-table) and apply production control units to set definite dates for each control step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select scheduling method to match task regularity and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheduling method depends on whether activities can be arranged in a standardized administrative sequence or consist of an assortment of tasks whose incidence cannot be exactly predicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For standardized recurrent processes schedule well in advance; for diversified or unpredictable workloads determine both time per task and frequency and use monthly work budgets or ad hoc schedules as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design plans emphasizing time and labor requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the plan emphasizing the time factor (including labor requirements) in each operation by reviewing work records and consulting division heads and technicians to determine tentative time estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tentative times should result from discussion and compromise with line officials, and times should be changed if operating experience shows them incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve line officials and professionals in accepting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards should be accepted by line officials; professional workers may resist but can agree when shown measurements and allowances for complexity and difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have conferences with division heads and technicians; incorporate their input so job times reflect agreed standards and can be revised with experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for backlog and motion delay; do not simply sum task times
rubrics_metrics.description: A common error is computing the time for a long job as the sum of individual task times when tasks are done in different units — this ignores motion delay and backlog, which determine additional time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make allowance for time in transit, processing, and especially the interval between delivery and the moment recipient starts work; account for backlog at each handling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure backlog empirically (control paper or diary method)
rubrics_metrics.description: An official's current backlog can be computed as the sum of job times for tasks on hand if estimated; average backlog may be discovered by a series of observations using the 'control paper' method or by maintaining and analyzing a work diary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange pending papers; note times when control paper reaches bottom; average intervals give backlog estimate; allow for variability and preferred handling types when interpreting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and limit priority/urgency categories
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is common to label papers 'rush', priority distinctions can lose meaning if overused; establish various levels of urgency only when needed and restrict expediting to extreme importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: German ministries have 'urgent matters' and 'immediate matters'; be cautious that too many 'rush' papers undermines discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth peaks by staffing and scheduling adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: To utilize energy and speed, straighten the flow of work and compensate for unavoidable peaks by assigning temporary employees and moving non-rush tasks to slack periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: stagger billings/paydays, schedule supply orders, start projects at regular intervals; these measures reduce peak overloads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare alternative schedules when overload exists ('should' vs 'will')
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of overload compile two schedules: one for work that should be done and one for work that will be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bad discrepancy supports requests for additional funds or reassignment of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include allowances for fatigue, unexpected jobs, and 'time for reflection'
rubrics_metrics.description: Work plans should consider special factors such as fatigue, incidence of unexpected jobs, miscellaneous minor tasks, travel time consolidation, and necessary time for reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan outside work for definite days but maintain flexibility for weather and other unpredictable factors; such allowances make work plans realistic and usually adhered to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, informative reports to show schedule status and delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must carry enough information to show whether work is proceeding on schedule and where delay is being encountered, yet be simple and easy to prepare, read, and interpret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sequences through divisions, current reports showing project status and directing attention to delays are most effective; reporting frequency should support timely production meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement a production control system (cards, flags, charts, meetings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A production control unit should file schedule cards showing due dates for actions; offices report weekly, post actions, attach warning/red flags for overdue items, stack and photograph cards, and produce charts showing current project status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send progress charts to administrators/division heads and hold regular production meetings to request explanations for delays and plan corrective action; remove uncontrollable items (e.g., litigation) from schedule temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use production meetings to analyze causes and plan corrective steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Production meetings are held to request explanations of delays and agree on steps to bring work back on schedule; they are intended to diagnose and correct faults rather than harry the delinquent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings should emphasize planning necessary action to restore schedule and spur divisional officials to timely performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report individual performance against schedules using working instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When scheduling is applied to individual workloads, performance should be reported in terms of the schedule by issuing working instructions with estimated job-times and deadlines; report by checking jobs done and entering time spent on major assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method (used by Forest Service) covers each man's workload as a whole and yields reports useful for evaluating and redistributing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consolidated work plans for many small tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing a consolidated work plan and completing it as a report is best for loads consisting of large numbers of small tasks where the character but not the exact incidence is known; useful for determining if employee has too little, just enough, or too much to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete consolidated plans periodically to evaluate workloads and reassign work as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track sizable non-recurrent jobs individually (card/percentage systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an employee whose work consists of a few sizable non-recurrent jobs, keep track of each separately using visible index cards showing title, date assigned, employee symbol, date due, and a percentage scale for reporting progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TVA system uses two strips (orange for percent completed, blue for time elapsed); periodic photographic reporting of masked cards yields exact status of projects and shows which employees can take more assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the administrative analyst with current unit capacity and work volume
rubrics_metrics.description: For scheduling non-routine centralized operations the analyst must have full advance information regarding the progress of current business and the volume of work on hand in each unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a 'Unit Production Chart' indicating capacity of each unit in man-hours by occupational classification and volume expected during forthcoming production period; adapt chart to office needs (professional units by individual, clerical by group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyst determines how tasks are done; do not usurp administrative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative analyst should not usurp the function of the administrator (who decides what is to be done); the analyst must determine how it is to be done — specifying functions, tasks, sequences, distribution, timing, and scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyst needs enough technical knowledge to size up operations, a fund of information on similar tasks, and the ability to outline new tasks clearly for estimating time requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise standards and schedules based on operating experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Job times and schedules should be changed if operating experience shows them to be incorrect; schedules may be revised as circumstances warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards should be adjusted only when justified by experience; the general psychological effect of reporting and meetings is to spur timely work and avoid excuses.
